([za.investing.com](https://za.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-slip-on-teetering-iran-ceasefire-as-trump-heads-to-china-4275164?utm_source=openai))

That level is materially below the war’s peak panic spikes but still far above prewar norms. Reuters reporting earlier in the conflict showed Brent above $100 after the blockade announcement and later near $114 during renewed hostilities; HSBC has since raised its 2026 average Brent forecast to $95 because of the longer effective closure of Hormuz. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-jump-6-to-above-100-a-barrel-on-us-blockade-of-iran-4610921?utm_source=openai))

Equity markets have shown more resilience than energy markets. Reuters reported in mid-April that Wall Street repeatedly treated any hint of renewed talks as a reason to rally, and other market coverage this week indicated U.S. equities remained near highs even as crude stayed volatile. The key structural point is that investors are increasingly treating the Iran war as a commodity shock and shipping shock rather than a generalized global-financial crisis—unless the conflict broadens again. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-shares-scale-sixweek-peak-on-hopes-for-usiran-peace-talks-4614170?utm_source=openai))

The second-order economic consequences remain substantial. Reuters said the Hormuz disruption stranded millions of barrels per day of Middle Eastern energy exports and that traffic is not expected to return to pre-conflict levels until later in 2026. That has fed inflation risk in import-dependent economies, widened freight and insurance costs, and increased the premium on geopolitical headlines. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-governments-energy-arm-assumes-strait-of-hormuz-will-stay-shut-through-late-may-4427981?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer story is no longer theoretical: supply-chain stress is spreading outward from the energy chokepoint. AP reported this week that the closure of Hormuz has squeezed bunker-fuel supply, especially affecting Singapore’s role as Asia’s largest marine refueling hub, with implications for shipping costs, consumer prices, and the movement of the roughly 80% of globally traded goods carried by sea. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0?utm_source=openai))

Reuters reported on May 12 that the U.S. Energy Information Administration assumes Hormuz will stay effectively shut through late May, and that export flows through the waterway, which handled about one-fifth of global oil supplies before the war, are not expected to normalize quickly. That implies continued strain for refiners, shipping firms, and importers across Asia-Pacific. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-governments-energy-arm-assumes-strait-of-hormuz-will-stay-shut-through-late-may-4427981?utm_source=openai))

AP also reported that Asia is bracing for a “second wave” of energy shocks, with the UN Development Programme estimating the conflict could impose $299 billion in losses on the Asia-Pacific region and push 8.8 million people toward poverty. While the user specifically asked about fuel hoarding, I found no high-confidence, independently confirmed Reuters or official last-24-hour report documenting fresh retail panic-buying lines at service stations today, May 14. The more defensible assessment is that governments and businesses are stockpiling and rerouting, while public hoarding remains episodic and poorly quantified in reliable reporting. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

There is also a broader cargo effect beyond petroleum. Reporting indicates the U.N. is seeking ways to secure fertilizer shipments to vulnerable countries, underscoring that the conflict is now a food-security and industrial-input problem as much as an oil problem. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/environment/article/2026/05/12/strait-of-hormuz-un-seeks-to-secure-fertilizer-shipments-to-fragile-countries-to-prevent-famines_6753380_114.html?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy remains active but brittle. AP reported that talks were expected on May 14-15, while Reuters and other reporting over recent days suggest mediation channels remain centered on Pakistan, with the U.S. and Iran still exchanging proposals even after Trump rejected Tehran’s latest package as unacceptable. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fdc6d2ae9396377919c967746fa9996b?utm_source=openai))

Trump’s own language has been contradictory: he says he wants a deal, but he has also framed the ceasefire as nearly dead. That ambiguity appears intentional. It preserves coercive leverage while avoiding a formal declaration that would force an immediate political choice between renewed full-scale war and visible compromise. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c?utm_source=openai))

At the multilateral level, the U.N. has consistently pushed for de-escalation, though there is no newly identified Security Council breakthrough in the last 24 hours. Reuters previously reported Secretary-General António Guterres judged it “highly probable” that talks would restart, and China has publicly argued that maintaining the ceasefire is an urgent necessity. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/uns-guterres-says-highly-probable-iran-talks-will-restart-4613483?utm_source=openai))

China and Russia continue to favor a diplomatic track that limits U.S. freedom of action while preserving their own influence. Reuters noted earlier this week that the Iran war was expected to loom over the May 14-15 Trump-Xi summit, highlighting how the conflict now intersects with wider great-power competition. Gulf states remain publicly cautious, seeking shipping security and de-escalation while avoiding direct exposure to Iranian retaliation. ([whtc.com](https://whtc.com/2026/05/11/factbox-iran-war-raises-stakes-for-us-and-china-ahead-of-trump-xi-talks/?utm_source=openai))

Net assessment: negotiations are still alive, but as of Thursday, May 14, 2026, there is no confirmed ceasefire breakthrough in the last 24 hours. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a major new humanitarian-access breakthrough or an authoritative updated civilian casualty total. The most credible standing estimates in open reporting remain severe: Reuters reported in April that Iranian authorities said more than 3,000 people had been killed in Iran during the war, while UNHCR said up to 3.2 million people had been displaced internally. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/aid-groups-use-land-routes-to-deliver-humanitarian-relief-to-iran-4612702?utm_source=openai))

Those figures are dated, but still important because they define the scale of unmet need. UNHCR has warned that displacement likely continued rising as hostilities and return pressures persisted, and its May situation materials indicate sustained concern about cross-border impacts and regional preparedness. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/ar/documents/download/122352?utm_source=openai))

Humanitarian access remains constrained by the conflict’s geography and logistics. Reuters reported that aid groups were forced to use overland routes for some of the first relief deliveries into Iran after the air war and maritime disruption made normal channels difficult. That suggests the blockade and shipping insecurity are compounding civilian harm indirectly, by slowing medical supply delivery and raising costs for relief operations. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/aid-groups-use-land-routes-to-deliver-humanitarian-relief-to-iran-4612702?utm_source=openai))

There is also a widening civilian impact beyond Iran itself. AP and other reporting on energy and shipping disruptions indicate that lower-income, import-dependent states are increasingly vulnerable to knock-on shortages in fuel, fertilizer, and transport-linked essentials. In intelligence terms, the humanitarian crisis is shifting from acute kinetic damage to a prolonged attritional phase defined by displacement, access constraints, and economic deprivation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: Watch three things on Day 76: whether the May 14-15 diplomatic window produces even a limited shipping or deconfliction arrangement, whether CENTCOM issues a new operational release indicating fresh maritime clashes, and whether oil breaks decisively away from the roughly $107 Brent area on either escalation or credible de-escalation signals. If talks fail without a face-saving interim mechanism on Hormuz, the probability of renewed U.S.-Iran combat in the next 24-72 hours will rise sharply. ([za.investing.com](https://za.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-slip-on-teetering-iran-ceasefire-as-trump-heads-to-china-4275164?utm_source=openai))

briefingArchive.title: Day 74 Intelligence Briefing — May 13, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development in the past 24 hours is diplomatic rather than kinetic: U.S.-Iran ceasefire diplomacy appears to be deteriorating, with President Trump describing the truce as effectively on “life support,” while Tehran rejected the latest U.S. proposal and continued to insist on wider conditions tied to sanctions, reparations and control of Hormuz. At the same time, shipping and energy disruption remain the war’s most strategically consequential effect, with fresh reporting indicating that Asian fuel systems and maritime bunker supply are under mounting strain as the Strait of Hormuz remains functionally constrained. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/12/hopes-fade-for-iran-peace-deal-as-trump-says-ceasefire-on-life-support?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

No major new confirmed U.S. or Iranian strike packages were publicly documented in the last 24 hours by primary military channels. The most recent official U.S. operational disclosure remains CENTCOM’s May 7 statement that U.S. Navy destroyers USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta, and USS Mason transiting the Strait of Hormuz intercepted Iranian missiles, drones, and small boats, after which U.S. forces struck Iranian missile and drone launch sites, command-and-control nodes, and ISR facilities; CENTCOM said no U.S. assets were hit. A subsequent May 8 CENTCOM release said U.S. forces disabled two Iranian-flagged unladen oil tankers attempting to enter Iranian ports in violation of the U.S. blockade. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

Within the last day, the operational picture is therefore best assessed as one of armed coercive standoff rather than renewed large-scale escalation. The U.S. continues to frame naval enforcement and retaliatory strikes as defensive measures tied to freedom of navigation and blockade enforcement, while Iran continues to use the strait as its principal strategic lever. Reporting over the past 24 hours indicates no confirmed new air campaign on the scale seen earlier in the war, no confirmed large missile salvos against Israel or Gulf capitals, and no fresh Pentagon release detailing additional weapon-system employment. In intelligence terms, the war’s center of gravity remains maritime: sea-lane control, interdiction, escort, and signaling. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a decisive territorial or operational shift by either side. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Relea-?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s public line remains that the United States has the situation militarily contained while still leaving open the possibility of renewed force. In comments reported over the last 24 hours, Trump said the U.S. has Iran “very much under control,” while AP reported that he also continued to threaten harsher action if Tehran does not agree to terms on its nuclear program and the broader war settlement. Earlier official CENTCOM language described Iranian attacks on U.S. ships as “unprovoked” and emphasized that U.S. strikes were self-defense actions against launch sites and command nodes. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/f3d5738853111cfc80985c157edab7c3?utm_source=openai))

Iranian messaging is sharply different. IRNA and other Iranian state channels portray the war as an illegal U.S.-Israeli aggression, reject U.S. maritime claims, and continue to insist that diplomacy must address not just de-escalation but sanctions relief, war reparations, and Iran’s claimed rights in Hormuz. IRNA’s archive also highlights repeated Iranian accusations of war crimes, including earlier allegations over attacks on schools and civilian infrastructure, and recent Iranian statements say reviewing the U.S. response to Tehran’s peace proposal is difficult given Washington’s conduct. ([lite.irna.ir](https://lite.irna.ir/en/allnews/?utm_source=openai))

The contradiction is straightforward: the U.S. describes a stabilizing enforcement operation; Iran describes an unlawful blockade and coercive war under cover of diplomacy. Israel has been less prominent in the last 24 hours’ reporting than Washington and Tehran, but the broader Israeli line remains aligned with the U.S. position that military pressure must continue until Iran’s threat capacity is durably reduced. The propaganda pattern is now familiar: U.S. statements stress precision, legality, and defensive response; Iranian outlets stress sovereignty, civilian harm, and strategic endurance. Neither side’s claims about deterrence success should be accepted at face value without corroboration. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remains the clearest real-time market barometer of conflict risk. Reuters reporting published May 12 said the Hormuz standoff was pushing oil higher again as hopes for a peace deal faded; separate Reuters-based market reporting also said Saudi crude exports to China are expected to fall further in June because buyers cut nominations amid high prices linked to the U.S.-Iran conflict and lower supply availability. While the freshest open search results did not expose full settlement tables for May 13, the latest Reuters-derived price point available in current search results showed Brent at $101.26 a barrel on May 8 during renewed hostilities, with the broader pattern this week pointing to persistent triple-digit pricing under war-risk conditions. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/12/hormuz-standoff-drives-oil-higher-as-iran-us-peace-hopes-ebb-2?utm_source=openai))

Equities are reacting less as if a fresh regional war has begun than as if a chronic energy-security shock is being repriced. Earlier Reuters market reporting showed U.S. stocks rallying when traders believed the war was nearing containment; that optimism has weakened as ceasefire hopes have ebbed again. The present market message is that investors still view Hormuz disruption, not Iranian long-range strike capacity, as the main macroeconomic transmission channel. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-shares-scale-sixweek-peak-on-hopes-for-usiran-peace-talks-4614170?utm_source=openai))

The second-order effects are increasingly visible. Reuters-based reporting indicates European fossil-fuel bills had already risen sharply earlier in the crisis, and current Asian buying patterns suggest refiners are still adjusting nominations and sourcing. Commodity stress is therefore extending beyond crude into shipping fuels and regional gas balances. In analytic terms, unless there is a verified reopening of normal maritime flows, oil is likely to remain structurally elevated and highly headline-sensitive. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours point to a decisive market stabilization. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-jump-6-to-above-100-a-barrel-on-us-blockade-of-iran-4562064?ampMode=1&utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer-facing impact is becoming more visible in Asia-Pacific, especially through marine fuel, import anxiety, and precautionary buying behavior. AP reported in the last 24 hours that the closure and militarization of Hormuz have choked bunker-fuel supply to Asia’s major maritime refueling hub, raising fears of downstream shortages in the shipping industry. A separate AP report from May 11 said Asia is bracing for a “second wave” of energy shocks as the conflict’s duration compounds the initial disruption caused by the strait’s closure. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/db0ba1dbc0bd3ff2179a84118d0064d0?utm_source=openai))

The most consequential new supply-chain reporting came from Reuters on May 12, which said Iraq and Pakistan had cut arrangements with Iran to move oil and LNG from the Gulf, demonstrating Tehran’s continued practical influence over energy flows through Hormuz. That matters because it suggests commercial actors are no longer merely waiting for a military solution; they are beginning to adapt to a politically mediated, fragmented shipping regime. Reuters previously noted that roughly 20% of global oil and gas exports normally transit Hormuz, with Asia the main destination region. ([gcaptain.com](https://gcaptain.com/iraq-and-pakistan-strike-iran-transit-deals-to-move-oil-and-lng-through-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

Direct evidence of mass retail gasoline hoarding across Asia in the last 24 hours remains limited in authoritative reporting. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours were found of large, verified civilian gas-station lines on the scale seen in earlier crisis phases. But the supply picture is still deteriorating in practical terms: reduced Gulf exports to Asian buyers, disrupted bunker-fuel distribution, and persistent uncertainty for shipping schedules all point toward continued pressure on freight rates, fuel inventories, and consumer costs in import-dependent economies. ([brecorder.com](https://www.brecorder.com/news/40420771?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy worsened over the last 24 hours. Reuters reported on May 12 that hopes for a peace agreement were fading after Trump said the ceasefire was on “life support,” while Tehran rejected the latest U.S. proposal and held to demands Washington characterized as unacceptable. That is the day’s key diplomatic indicator: negotiations are not dead, but neither side is currently signaling readiness for a narrow technical compromise. ([internazionale.it](https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-notizie-reuters/2026/05/12/hopes-fade-for-iran-peace-deal-as-trump-says-ceasefire-on-life-support?utm_source=openai))

China remains central to U.S. strategy, at least rhetorically. AP reported that Trump traveled to Beijing while saying he expected a long discussion with Xi Jinping, though he also downplayed differences and suggested trade would overshadow Iran in the talks. AP separately reported that Washington has been trying, unsuccessfully so far, to use China’s leverage to pressure Tehran into either accepting U.S. terms or at minimum reopening Hormuz. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/48b0ca751712ce473ffcd207997928af?utm_source=openai))

At the UN, the main recent line has been pressure on Iran over Hormuz. UN reporting from May 7 said the U.S. and Bahrain circulated a Security Council draft calling on Iran to cease attacks in the strait. But the broader diplomatic backdrop is difficult: China and Russia previously vetoed a Hormuz-related resolution in April, showing that the Security Council remains structurally divided. Gulf states remain aligned with Washington on maritime security, though their own exposure to retaliation constrains their room for maneuver. Back-channel diplomacy via Pakistan remains active in principle, but no confirmed breakthrough was reported in the last 24 hours. ([dppa.dfs.un.org](https://dppa.dfs.un.org/en/bahrain-and-us-float-security-council-resolution-strait-of-hormuz?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No authoritative humanitarian agency appears to have published a major new Iran-specific casualty update in the last 24 hours. The most recent broad UNHCR estimate still indicates that up to 3.2 million people may be temporarily displaced inside Iran, with many moving from Tehran and other cities toward northern and rural areas; that figure is dated March 12 and should be treated as a baseline rather than a current tally. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/de/news/pressemitteilungen/iran-bis-zu-3-2-millionen-menschen-voruebergehend-vertrieben?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC warned on April 30 that any return to large-scale warfare would be ruinous for civilians, noting that six weeks of hostilities had already devastated infrastructure people rely on to survive. UN-linked humanitarian reporting has also warned of attacks on hospitals, schools, water systems, power facilities, and aid workers across the regional theater, including Iran. These are not fresh daily casualty figures, but they remain the most credible available indicators of humanitarian stress in the absence of new verified field tallies today. ([icrc.org](https://www.icrc.org/en/news-release/iran-icrc-president-says-return-war-would-be-ruinous-civilians?utm_source=openai))

Iranian state media continue to foreground civilian harm allegations, including earlier claims regarding school strikes and child casualties. Those figures cannot be independently verified from the last 24 hours through the sources reviewed here, and should therefore be treated as claims rather than confirmed totals. The most defensible current assessment is that humanitarian conditions remain severe, displacement remains large-scale, and civilian infrastructure damage is extensive, but there are no confirmed reports in the last 24 hours of a new mass-casualty event that materially changes the overall picture. ([lite.irna.ir](https://lite.irna.ir/en/allnews/?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The main indicators for May 14 are whether Trump’s Beijing diplomacy yields any Chinese pressure on Tehran, whether Tehran signals flexibility on Hormuz access, and whether either side resumes publicly acknowledged strikes after the current political hardening. Markets will watch crude first and military statements second; if there is no diplomatic movement, the next escalation is more likely to emerge at sea than through a headline-grabbing strategic bombing campaign. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/48b0ca751712ce473ffcd207997928af?utm_source=openai))

briefingArchive.title: Day 73 Intelligence Briefing — May 12, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development in the past 24 hours is political rather than kinetic: President Donald Trump said the U.S.-Iran ceasefire is on “life support,” while U.S. officials signaled he is weighing renewed military action to pressure Tehran. Markets have reacted immediately, with Brent crude rising above $104 a barrel, even as there were no newly confirmed large-scale U.S. or Israeli strike packages announced in the last 24 hours. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c))

## Military Operations Summary

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a fresh major wave of U.S. or Israeli airstrikes comparable to earlier phases of Operation Epic Fury. The latest confirmed U.S. military operational disclosure remains CENTCOM’s May 7 statement that U.S. forces protected three Navy guided-missile destroyers — USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta, and USS Mason — during a Strait of Hormuz transit, intercepting Iranian missiles, drones, and small boats before conducting self-defense strikes on Iranian missile and drone launch sites, command-and-control nodes, and ISR facilities. CENTCOM’s public releases page shows no newer Iran-related press release after May 8, when it reported disabling two more vessels violating the U.S. blockade in the Gulf of Oman. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/?utm_source=openai))

The operational picture over the last 24 hours therefore appears to be one of armed pause under a failing truce rather than full resumption of open war. Axios reported on May 11 that Trump is considering some form of military action and may also resume “Project Freedom,” the suspended U.S. escort mission intended to guide shipping through Hormuz. That suggests U.S. force posture remains offensive-capable and that naval escort operations are the most likely near-term flashpoint. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/11/trump-iran-ceasefile-military-action))

On the Iranian side, state-linked outlets continue to emphasize deterrence at sea rather than acknowledge battlefield losses. Press TV and IRNA messaging in recent days has stressed Iranian control over designated shipping corridors and warnings that unauthorized military approaches to Hormuz will be met forcefully. Taken together, the last 24 hours show no confirmed new strategic bombing campaign, but a high-risk environment in which naval incidents, blockade enforcement, and escort operations could rapidly trigger renewed combat. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/05/768106/Iran-IRGC-warning-sailing-Hormuz-Strait-routes?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s line remains that the ceasefire technically still exists, but is close to collapse because of Iranian intransigence. Trump said on May 11 that the ceasefire was on “life support,” and AP reported the White House sees recent exchanges of fire and stalled diplomacy as capable of tipping the region back into open warfare. Axios went further, citing U.S. officials who said Trump is leaning toward renewed military action to force concessions on Iran’s nuclear program. CENTCOM’s most recent operational statement framed prior U.S. action in the Strait as defensive and limited, saying American forces intercepted “unprovoked Iranian attacks” and struck only facilities directly tied to those attacks. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c))

Iranian state messaging sharply contradicts that version. IRNA’s English service says Iran’s UN ambassador accused the United States of violating the April 8 ceasefire through military action against Iranian tankers and coastal targets. Press TV has repeatedly rejected U.S. claims about Hormuz transits and portrays Iran as the legitimate authority regulating maritime movement, not the disruptor. Iranian outlets also frame any U.S. escort or blockade operation as “aggression” and insist the only durable solution is ending the war and lifting maritime pressure. ([www2.irna.ir](https://www2.irna.ir/en?utm_source=openai))

Israeli public reporting in the past 24 hours has been comparatively muted on fresh operations, with commentary focused more on preventing Iranian recovery than on announcing new strikes. The contradiction across narratives is clear: the U.S. depicts calibrated self-defense and pressure for a deal; Iran depicts illegal ceasefire violations and sovereign maritime enforcement; Israel continues to argue that de-escalation without strategic rollback of Iran would be a mistake. All three information streams contain obvious propagandistic elements, especially casualty opacity, legal framing, and competing claims over control of Hormuz. ([israelhayom.com](https://www.israelhayom.com/2026/04/11/israels-challenge-is-stopping-irans-recovery/?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Energy remains the clearest real-time barometer of escalation risk. AP reported that Brent crude rose 2.9% on May 11 to settle at $104.21 a barrel after Trump said the ceasefire was on “life support.” The same report said the war has pushed Brent up from roughly $70 before the conflict, underlining how much of the global inflation shock remains tied to the prolonged disruption of Gulf shipping and uncertainty over Hormuz. Earlier hopes for de-escalation had briefly pulled Brent down toward $101, but that relief has proven fragile. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/234022685a51477ea9f72cc5aa170829))

Equities have been more resilient than energy. AP said U.S. stocks still edged toward records despite the renewed oil spike, indicating investors continue to price in either eventual de-escalation or manageable containment rather than a worst-case regional war. Even so, energy-sensitive sectors, transport, airlines, and import-dependent Asian economies remain under visible pressure. Reuters reporting earlier in the crisis also described the shock as large enough to flip expectations for the 2026 oil market from surplus to deficit, and to drive the biggest annual increase in analyst Brent forecasts on record. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/234022685a51477ea9f72cc5aa170829))

For consumers, the pass-through is already severe. AP reported last week that average U.S. regular gasoline reached $4.48 a gallon, up 31 cents in a week and roughly 50% above the pre-war level. That helps explain the White House discussion of a federal gas-tax pause. Gold and broader safe-haven positioning have also firmed amid the conflict, though the dominant macro variable remains oil. The market message today is straightforward: traders are no longer pricing a clean ceasefire path and are again assigning a premium to renewed military disruption. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e5b61be4a4c8a8a077ed5ff6f84c0ce?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The Asia-Pacific region remains the most exposed civilian-economic theater of the conflict. AP reported on May 11 that Asia’s initial emergency energy measures are running out of room, with a “second wave” of effects now hitting: higher utility bills, rising shipping costs, elevated airfares, and pressure on growth. The same report, citing UNDP, said about 8.8 million people are at risk of being pushed into poverty and that the conflict could impose $299 billion in losses across Asia-Pacific. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6))

On the ground, there is evidence of sustained stress rather than a single panic event. AP described governments across Asia redirecting fuel supplies, drawing down stockpiles, and prioritizing household gas over industrial demand. In India, redirecting fuel toward roughly 330 million households has cut into fertilizer supply, creating second-order food-security and inflation risks. Earlier reporting from the region documented cooking-gas shortages, restaurant closures, and lines for LPG cylinders; current conditions suggest those emergency distortions are becoming entrenched. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45dcf2b9059930f298136720564d6ae6))

Shipping disruption through Hormuz remains central. AP reported that hundreds of vessels are still stuck in the Persian Gulf and that major ship operators continue to judge the strait too dangerous. Before the war, 100 to 135 vessels transited Hormuz daily, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence cited by AP; traffic has since fallen to a trickle. Some ships face Iranian routing requirements near the coast and disclosure demands on cargo and crew, while others avoid entry altogether because of drone, missile, speedboat, and insurance risk. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a broad restoration of normal shipping flows. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/03af894eaddb8ede53928babc76f80e2))

## Diplomatic Developments

The main diplomatic development in the past 24 hours is deterioration, not breakthrough. Trump publicly rejected Iran’s latest proposal and said the ceasefire is on “life support,” while Axios reported he is weighing renewed military action. That combination suggests the White House now sees coercive leverage, not compromise, as the more likely path to movement. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c))

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours show a ceasefire deal, formal resumption of Islamabad-style talks, or a new negotiated framework. The most recent publicly known diplomatic track remains the one-page U.S. framework previously referenced by Axios and the earlier Pakistan-mediated channel, both of which appear stalled. Iranian state media has continued to signal openness to diplomacy in principle, but only on terms that guarantee no renewed aggression and preserve core Iranian positions, including rights language around its nuclear program and opposition to the maritime blockade. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/06/trump-iran-war-deal-framework-response?utm_source=openai))

At the multilateral level, the UN’s line remains restraint. Recent UN messaging has called on all parties to abide by the ceasefire and avoid renewed escalation in the Strait of Hormuz. China has publicly called for the war to end and for Hormuz to reopen, while Russia continues rhetorical alignment with Tehran and coordination with Beijing on the crisis. Gulf states remain divided in tone but broadly alarmed by any return to open conflict, especially after earlier Iranian attacks and threats directed toward regional infrastructure and ports. The near-term diplomatic picture is therefore one of hardening positions, narrow mediator space, and growing risk that naval incidents overtake negotiations. ([aa.com.tr](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/world/un-urges-maximum-restraint-after-renewed-us-iran-escalation-in-strait-of-hormuz/3931857?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours provide a new consolidated casualty count for Iran or the wider theater. That absence is important: battlefield reporting remains heavily politicized, and neither U.S./Israeli nor Iranian sources are providing transparent, independently verified daily tolls. The safest assessment is that the humanitarian burden continues to deepen, but hard 24-hour numbers remain unconfirmed. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0e9067769efea20e9d45e3d43158ad8c))

The broader humanitarian picture remains grave. UNHCR’s latest regional update still lists 3.2 million people temporarily internally relocated in Iran according to government figures, while warning that armed hostilities and return pressures may force further onward movement, including among Afghans in Iran. Earlier UNHCR reporting had already flagged large-scale displacement from Tehran and the risk of expanding regional population flows. ([data.unhcr.org](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/download/122352))

The ICRC has continued to warn that any return to full-scale war would be ruinous for civilians. Its Iran delegation says it delivered 171 metric tonnes of emergency relief items to the Iranian Red Crescent in April, underscoring ongoing humanitarian need, and ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric warned during her Tehran visit that renewed fighting would have devastating civilian consequences. The humanitarian impact is not limited to direct deaths and injuries: damage to civilian infrastructure, energy systems, health services, and logistics networks is compounding vulnerability across Iran and neighboring states. In analytic terms, even in the absence of a fresh mass-casualty event in the last 24 hours, the crisis remains acute and structurally worsening. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/))

Outlook: Watch three indicators on May 13: whether the White House formally resumes “Project Freedom,” whether Iran adjusts its Hormuz maritime enforcement posture, and whether any mediator — likely Pakistan, Oman, or China — can reopen a channel before another naval clash forces escalation. Oil’s reaction around the $104 Brent level and any new CENTCOM or Iranian military communiqués will be the fastest signals of whether Day 74 is heading back toward open war. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/11/trump-iran-ceasefile-military-action))

briefingArchive.title: Day 72 Intelligence Briefing — May 11, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development over the last 24 hours is not a major new kinetic escalation, but the persistence of a fragile, highly militarized pause around the Strait of Hormuz while Washington awaits Tehran’s answer to a draft interim deal. That has kept oil and shipping markets volatile, even as the latest confirmed combat reporting still points to the May 7-8 naval-air exchange as the most recent clearly documented clash. ([iranintl.com](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605071506))

## Military Operations Summary

No major new confirmed U.S. or Iranian strikes were publicly documented in the last 24 hours ending May 11, 2026. The latest official U.S. military reporting remains CENTCOM’s May 8 statement that U.S. forces disabled two Iranian-flagged unladen tankers, M/T Sea Star III and M/T Sevda, before they could enter an Iranian port in the Gulf of Oman, using F/A-18 Super Hornets from USS George H.W. Bush and precision strikes into the vessels’ smokestacks. CENTCOM also said a third tanker, M/T Hasna, had been disabled on May 6 by an F/A-18 from USS Abraham Lincoln using 20mm cannon fire on the rudder. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480820/us-disables-2-more-vessels-violating-blockade-in-gulf-of-oman/))

The latest confirmed direct combat between state forces remains the May 7 Hormuz transit operation. CENTCOM said Iranian forces launched missiles, drones, and small boats at USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta, and USS Mason as they moved through the strait, and that U.S. forces then struck Iranian launch sites, command-and-control nodes, and ISR positions in self-defense. Press TV, by contrast, described the same episode as an Iranian naval success that forced U.S. destroyers to withdraw after attacks with anti-ship ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, drones, and rockets. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/))

Operationally, the military picture remains centered on maritime coercion rather than deep inland strike packages. Project Freedom, announced by CENTCOM on May 3, still frames U.S. force posture: guided-missile destroyers, more than 100 air assets, unmanned systems, and roughly 15,000 personnel tasked with restoring commercial navigation while simultaneously enforcing the blockade on Iranian shipping. In practice, however, there are no confirmed reports in the last 24 hours of a new escorted convoy, major carrier air wing strike, or fresh Israeli long-range air operation. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4476318/us-military-supports-launch-of-project-freedom-in-strait-of-hormuz/))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s line remains that recent actions are defensive, legal under self-defense, and tied to freedom of navigation. CENTCOM says it intercepted “unprovoked Iranian attacks” during the May 7 destroyer transit and targeted only the military infrastructure used to attack U.S. forces. It also presents the tanker interdictions as disciplined blockade enforcement rather than escalation, emphasizing precision fire and the disabling—not sinking—of vessels. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4480437/centcom-protects-us-warships-transiting-strait-of-hormuz/))

Iranian state messaging is sharply different. Press TV says Iranian naval forces struck U.S. destroyers and drove them away from Hormuz, portraying the United States as the ceasefire violator and Tehran as defending sovereign navigational rights. IRNA’s English and Farsi outputs similarly frame the U.S. naval blockade and attacks on tankers as illegal aggression; Iran’s U.N. envoy has formally called the attacks on the tankers and coastal sites a blatant violation of the April 8 ceasefire. IRNA also highlights Tehran’s position that the only viable route to normal passage is a permanent end to the war and lifting of the blockade. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/08/768247/Iran-Navy-repels-US-destroyers-from-Strait-of-Hormuz-as-Tehran-warns-bared-fangs-not-a-smile?utm_source=openai))

Third-party reporting suggests both sides are shaping narratives for diplomatic leverage. AP independently reported that the U.S. military said it intercepted Iranian attacks on three Navy ships and noted that hundreds of ships and thousands of mariners remain stranded, which broadly supports the scale of the maritime crisis but does not verify Iranian claims of damage to U.S. warships. Reuters reporting from May 5 also said U.S. intelligence assessed only limited damage to Iran’s nuclear program since the war began, undercutting some of the maximalist political claims around strategic effects. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fdc6d2ae9396377919c967746fa9996b))

Israeli public reporting appears more restrained over the last 24 hours, with no major new confirmed Israeli operational disclosure located in the available sources. That relative quiet may itself be significant: it suggests Israel is currently allowing the maritime and negotiating track between Washington and Tehran to dominate the information environment rather than advertising new independent strike activity. This is an analytical inference based on the absence of fresh confirmed Israeli announcements in current open sources. ([iranintl.com](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605071506))

## Market & Economic Impact

Energy markets remain the clearest real-time barometer of war risk. Brent has come off the early-May spike above $115, but it remains historically elevated and highly sensitive to any sign that Hormuz will stay shut or reopen only partially. AP reported Brent at $101.27 on May 6, then $100.06 on May 7, after ceasefire optimism improved; Reuters reported on May 8 that renewed fighting pushed WTI to $95.66 and that benchmarks had risen more than 3% at the open before paring gains. Earlier in the week, Reuters-cited market reporting said Brent was holding near $114 after fresh hostilities. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0da189a3d33b041087b7df6096e5c8ad?utm_source=openai))

The broader market reaction is a classic conflict-risk pattern: oil up on renewed fighting, equities up when traders believe diplomacy may reopen Hormuz. AP reported Wall Street records on easing oil and profit strength earlier in the week, followed by a retreat when crude “yo-yoed” and investors questioned whether peace-talk optimism was justified. Reuters market coverage likewise described global stocks as mixed on May 7 as oil fell on peace optimism, showing that macro sentiment is still being driven primarily by headlines from the strait and negotiation channel rather than by fundamentals alone. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/e1c194b5266c4eb58dc993cc4a9f9b50?utm_source=openai))

Analysts are also repricing the medium-term supply shock. Reuters-cited reports show Barclays raised its 2026 Brent forecast to $100 per barrel on prolonged Hormuz disruption, while ANZ expects Brent above $90 this year and finishing 2026 at $88 because of lasting Middle East supply losses. Barclays estimated a current market deficit of about 6.6 million barrels per day if disruption persists. Those are forecast numbers, not spot prices, but they underscore the market view that even a ceasefire would not quickly normalize flows. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/commodities-news/barclays-lifts-2026-brent-forecast-to-100-on-prolonged-hormuz-disruption-4604795?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The immediate supply-chain picture remains severe. Hundreds of vessels and tens of thousands of mariners are still effectively trapped by the Hormuz crisis, according to AP, and shipping companies continue to face shifting military guidance, insurance uncertainty, and physical risk from drones, missiles, mines, and fast boats. AP reported this week that a CMA CGM-operated container ship was damaged while attempting a transit, reinforcing industry reluctance to resume regular schedules even when military escorts are discussed. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/03af894eaddb8ede53928babc76f80e2?utm_source=openai))

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours establish fresh, large-scale consumer fuel hoarding episodes in Asia-Pacific. But the structural drivers remain in place. Reuters previously documented suspended oil and LNG shipments via Hormuz, while its fuel-shortage and LNG-crisis coverage indicates the war has already pushed Asian importers into an acute energy-security posture. Because roughly one-fifth of global oil and large volumes of LNG normally transit Hormuz, Asia remains the most exposed end market, especially for price-sensitive importers and LNG-dependent economies. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-and-gas-majors-and-traders-suspend-shipments-via-hormuz-as-us-attacks-iran-sources-say-4533427?utm_source=openai))

Operationally, the key question is not whether a route exists, but whether commercial operators believe it is insurable and survivable. Reuters reported that even when limited escorted passages occurred, shipping data showed only a small number of tankers moved before restrictions snapped back. That implies continued dislocation in tanker scheduling, freight rates, bunker costs, and downstream refinery planning across Asia. An important indicator for tomorrow is whether any major liner, tanker, or LNG operator publicly resumes Hormuz transits at scale; as of now, there is no confirmed evidence of such a shift in the last 24 hours. ([za.investing.com](https://za.investing.com/news/world-news/some-tankers-cross-strait-of-hormuz-before-shots-fired-shiptracking-data-shows-4219216?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomatically, the center of gravity is the proposed interim U.S.-Iran arrangement now reportedly under Iranian review. Reuters, via Iran International, said the two sides were working toward a one-page memorandum that would formally end the war, address the Strait of Hormuz crisis, and create a 30-day window for broader negotiations while leaving major disputes unresolved. AP reported on May 9 that Washington was awaiting Tehran’s response to its latest proposal, and that Moscow’s offer to remove enriched uranium from Iran remained on the table as part of a possible settlement mechanism. ([iranintl.com](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605071506))

The United Nations has continued to call for full adherence to the ceasefire. IRNA reported U.N. spokesman Farhan Haq urging all parties to avoid actions that could reignite tensions or undermine diplomacy, particularly in Hormuz. Iran is using that language to reinforce its argument that U.S. strikes on tankers and coastal targets are ceasefire violations; Washington, by contrast, continues to frame its actions as defensive enforcement and maritime security operations. ([www2.irna.ir](https://www2.irna.ir/news/86148968/?utm_source=openai))

China and Russia remain positioned as diplomatic beneficiaries of prolonged U.S.-Iran deadlock. IRNA says Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi welcomed a four-point Chinese proposal after talks in Beijing, while AP says Putin has kept his uranium-removal proposal available. Gulf states remain publicly cautious; the regional mood appears to favor de-escalation, restoration of shipping, and avoidance of being drawn further into the conflict. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a finalized ceasefire expansion, signed memorandum, or new direct talks round. ([lite.irna.ir](https://lite.irna.ir/en/?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No major new internationally verified casualty update was located for the last 24 hours. The most authoritative baseline available in open source remains the U.N. humanitarian update for Iran, which said as of March 17 that more than 1,200 people had been killed and over 17,000 injured, with casualties and civilian infrastructure damage reported in at least 20 provinces. The U.N. also said airstrikes had damaged fuel depots, a desalination plant, and other critical infrastructure, while forcing millions to relocate internally. ([iran.un.org](https://iran.un.org/en/313396-islamic-republic-iran-humanitarian-update-no-01-17-march-2026))

The ICRC has warned that a return to major combat would be ruinous for civilians and has already delivered 171 metric tonnes of emergency relief items to the Iranian Red Crescent. Its Iran mission reporting also notes the killing of multiple Iranian Red Crescent personnel and volunteers in earlier strikes, underscoring the cumulative danger to humanitarian responders even during lulls in fighting. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/))

What is missing from the last 24 hours is almost as important as what is present: there is no fresh, independently verified humanitarian snapshot from U.N. agencies, ICRC, or major NGOs covering new displacement, hospital overload, or updated casualty counts following the latest Hormuz fighting. That likely reflects access, verification delays, and the fact that the most recent confrontation has been predominantly maritime. Even so, the indirect humanitarian effects remain serious: fuel disruption, economic shock, and prolonged uncertainty are continuing to degrade civilian welfare across Iran and the wider region. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/))

Outlook: The primary indicator for May 12 will be whether Tehran formally answers the U.S. interim proposal and whether that response produces a measurable change in shipping behavior through Hormuz. Absent a diplomatic breakthrough, the most likely near-term pattern is continued low-level maritime confrontation, information warfare over ceasefire violations, and renewed oil-price volatility on even minor operational incidents.

briefingArchive.title: Day 71 Intelligence Briefing — May 10, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development over the past 24 hours is not a major new battlefield breakthrough, but the apparent holding of a fragile ceasefire amid continued brinkmanship around the Strait of Hormuz and renewed warnings from Tehran over attacks on its shipping. Markets remain highly sensitive to any hint that the truce could fail, with oil still elevated and maritime traffic through Hormuz far below normal levels. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0c25b2ca53ee90bc19bfbf6c44a66e6e?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a large new round of US-Israeli deep strikes inside Iran comparable to earlier phases of Operation Epic Fury. The operational picture is instead defined by deterrent posturing, maritime coercion, and the aftereffects of the May 7–8 exchange in and around the Strait of Hormuz. AP reported today, May 10, that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy warned any attack on Iranian oil tankers or commercial shipping would trigger a “heavy assault” on a US base in the region and on enemy vessels, while the ceasefire appeared to remain in place. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0c25b2ca53ee90bc19bfbf6c44a66e6e?utm_source=openai))

The most recent confirmed kinetic activity still dates to May 7–8. AP reported that US forces said they intercepted Iranian attacks on three Navy ships in the Strait of Hormuz and then struck Iranian military facilities allegedly responsible for those attacks. Earlier in the week, AP also reported the US military said it sank six Iranian small boats targeting civilian ships during efforts to reopen the strait. Iranian media, by contrast, described missile, drone, and rocket fire as warning action that repelled US destroyers and damaged intruding vessels. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fdc6d2ae9396377919c967746fa9996b?utm_source=openai))

The standing US military posture remains centered on maritime access and blockade enforcement rather than a publicly declared renewed air campaign. CENTCOM’s latest available 2026 releases confirm a blockade of traffic entering or leaving Iranian ports and prior mine-clearance and escort operations involving guided-missile destroyers such as USS Frank E. Peterson and USS Michael Murphy. No fresh CENTCOM press release visible in the last 24 hours publicly announces new strike packages, specific bomb damage assessments, or additional weapon-system employment. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4457255/us-to-blockade-ships-entering-or-exiting-iranian-ports/?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s public line remains that major combat under Operation Epic Fury is over, but limited military action remains available to protect shipping, enforce the blockade, and respond to attacks below the threshold of full war resumption. ABC reported earlier this week that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Operation Epic Fury is “over” and that US policy has shifted toward “Project Freedom” and restoring movement through Hormuz. AP separately reported Pentagon briefers said the ceasefire still held despite multiple Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and US forces since early April. ([abcnews.com](https://abcnews.com/Politics/rubio-operation-iran-nuclear-material-removed/story?id=132687267&utm_source=openai))

US and coalition claims emphasize precision, legality, and defensive necessity. AP’s May 7 reporting said the US military intercepted Iranian attacks on three Navy ships and targeted the Iranian facilities responsible. CENTCOM’s standing statements frame Iranian port and maritime infrastructure as dual-use nodes employed for military activity and therefore legitimate targets under the law of armed conflict, while insisting non-Iranian commercial freedom of navigation remains the objective. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fdc6d2ae9396377919c967746fa9996b?utm_source=openai))

Iranian state and semi-state media present the opposite narrative: that the US blockade failed, that Tehran retains effective control over the strait, and that any missile or drone launches were lawful warning actions against ceasefire violations. Press TV has described recent US efforts as “adventurism,” claimed Iranian naval forces repelled US destroyers, and argued the American pivot from blockade to escorted transits reflected strategic failure rather than leverage. Today’s AP reporting similarly shows Iran warning that attacks on tankers would prompt direct retaliation against US regional bases. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/05/768091/failed-strait-blockade-forces-us-pivot-iran-strategic-patience-leverage-grow?utm_source=openai))

Israel’s reporting in the last 24 hours is comparatively muted in the publicly accessible reporting reviewed here. There are no confirmed Israeli official statements today detailing fresh independent strikes inside Iran. The main contradiction remains this: Washington says it is enforcing maritime security within a ceasefire framework; Tehran says those same actions are ceasefire breaches and proof that the war has not truly ended. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0c25b2ca53ee90bc19bfbf6c44a66e6e?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remains the clearest real-time barometer of conflict risk. Reuters reporting carried on May 8 said Brent crude futures rose to $101.47 a barrel and US WTI to $95.93 after renewed US-Iran hostilities. That followed earlier extreme volatility in late April and early May, when Reuters and Axios reported Brent had climbed above $111 and briefly topped $126 during peak fears of prolonged Hormuz disruption. The market has since pulled back from the highs, but the war premium remains substantial. ([geo.tv](https://www.geo.tv/latest/663392-oil-prices-jump-on-renewed-us-iran-hostilities?utm_source=openai))

Equity markets are reacting with more restraint than energy markets, but the tone remains cautious. Reuters reported on May 7 that US and European stocks slipped while oil swung sharply on alternating signals of confrontation and diplomacy. Another Reuters market roundup noted that Asian stocks were only slightly off record highs even after the latest exchange of fire, suggesting investors still see a meaningful probability of negotiated de-escalation rather than an immediate return to full-scale war. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-stocks-hit-record-high-dollar-wobbles-on-peace-deal-hopes-4615955?utm_source=openai))

The broader macro story is that oil volatility, not headline military damage, is driving pricing across asset classes. Reuters cited analysts warning that Brent remained roughly 40% above its late-February level, underscoring persistent inflationary pressure and the risk of a longer supply shock. Gold was also elevated enough to warrant safe-haven attention, though no confirmed last-24-hour breakout tied specifically to today’s developments was identified in the sources reviewed. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-stocks-hit-record-high-dollar-wobbles-on-peace-deal-hopes-4615955?utm_source=openai))

In practical terms, markets are trading the strait, not the battlefield. Any evidence that Hormuz can reopen sustainably would likely compress the geopolitical premium quickly; any attack on tankers, mine incident, or US-Iran exchange around escorts would probably push crude sharply higher again. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/most-strait-of-hormuz-shipping-at-a-standstill-despite-latest-us-pledge-4655862?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer impact remains most acute where refined-product supply chains are tight and maritime rerouting options are limited. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours establish new large-scale retail fuel hoarding episodes today, but Reuters has previously documented fuel shortages across parts of Asia as the war dragged on, and recent shipping reporting shows the core disruption remains unresolved. ([reutersconnect.com](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/timeline-fuel-shortages-across-asia-as-iran-war-drags-on/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1ZBNTE0NzE4MDMyMDI2UlAx/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX0xWQTAwMzUxNDcxODAzMjAyNlJQMQ?utm_source=openai))

The shipping picture is stark. Reuters reported on May 4 that most Strait of Hormuz shipping remained at a standstill despite US pledges to free up movement. Reuters also reported on April 29 that only six ships, a fraction of normal traffic, had crossed in 24 hours, while the US navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center assessed commercial traffic as still limited even after the April ceasefire. AP added on May 6 that hundreds of vessels were effectively stuck in the Gulf and that operators remained deterred by drones, small-boat threats, and projectile strikes. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/most-strait-of-hormuz-shipping-at-a-standstill-despite-latest-us-pledge-4655862?utm_source=openai))

That has direct knock-on effects for Asia-Pacific consumers. Reuters-linked timeline material indicates shortages and stress across Asian fuel markets as disrupted crude and LNG flows ripple through import-dependent economies. Although there is no fresh Reuters dispatch in the last 24 hours detailing new panic-buying lines at service stations, the persistence of near-standstill Hormuz traffic suggests the structural drivers for hoarding behavior remain in place: uncertain deliveries, volatile prices, and fears that governments may impose fuel management measures. ([reutersconnect.com](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/timeline-fuel-shortages-across-asia-as-iran-war-drags-on/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1ZBNTE0NzE4MDMyMDI2UlAx/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX0xWQTAwMzUxNDcxODAzMjAyNlJQMQ?utm_source=openai))

The supply-chain implication for tomorrow is simple: if the ceasefire holds but navigation remains politically contested, freight, insurance, and inventory costs will stay elevated even without headline-grabbing attacks. That is a slower-burning but economically potent form of disruption. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/03af894eaddb8ede53928babc76f80e2?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomatically, the center of gravity is now around a proposed deal that would end the war, reopen Hormuz, and address Iran’s nuclear program, but no final agreement has been announced in the last 24 hours. AP reported today that Washington is awaiting Tehran’s response to its latest proposal, even as Iranian military officials warn against attacks on tankers and bases. That combination suggests active back-channeling continues under the cover of deterrent rhetoric. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0c25b2ca53ee90bc19bfbf6c44a66e6e?utm_source=openai))

At the United Nations, the US and Gulf allies are still trying to mobilize pressure on Iran over shipping. AP reported this week that they circulated a draft UN resolution threatening sanctions or other measures if Iran does not stop attacks on ships, end alleged illegal tolling, and disclose mine locations. Reuters reported on May 7 that China and Russia were likely to veto the measure, illustrating the continuing diplomatic split inside the Security Council. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fb9532308885dd260bf8f44353d51b0a?utm_source=openai))

The UN Secretariat’s public stance remains de-escalatory. UN reporting from the May 6 closed-door Security Council session reiterated support for peace efforts as the Hormuz crisis continued. Earlier UN statements by Secretary-General António Guterres called for continued talks and an end to ceasefire violations, and there is no indication from the last 24 hours that the UN has shifted away from that line. ([un.org](https://www.un.org/en/security-council-holds-closed-door-talks-following-attacks-united-arab-emirates?utm_source=openai))

China’s position, based on the latest available Reuters reporting, is consistent: restraint, renewed dialogue, and opposition to measures that could further militarize the strait. Russia appears aligned with Beijing in resisting the US-backed UN approach. Gulf states remain publicly supportive of freedom of navigation and more coercive pressure on Tehran, though they also have strong incentives to avoid becoming direct targets again. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/china-urges-restraint-over-us-blockade-of-strait-of-hormuz-backs-talks-4609452?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No confirmed last-24-hour humanitarian bulletin reviewed here provides a materially updated casualty or displacement total for today, May 10. The humanitarian picture therefore remains best understood through the latest standing data rather than fresh figures. UNHCR said in March that up to 3.2 million people were temporarily displaced inside Iran, and its regional tracking page continues to describe elevated internal displacement and precautionary cross-border movements driven by ongoing military operations. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/us/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC has warned repeatedly that any return to high-intensity war would be catastrophic for civilians. In a statement published last week after a senior visit to Iran, ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric said renewed conflict would be “ruinous for civilians,” reflecting concern that the ceasefire’s fragility leaves millions exposed to renewed strikes on transport, energy, and urban infrastructure. ([icrc.org](https://www.icrc.org/en/news-release/iran-icrc-president-says-return-war-would-be-ruinous-civilians?utm_source=openai))

Aid access remains constrained but not fully severed. Reuters reported in mid-April that humanitarian groups had begun moving emergency supplies overland into Iran and through the Iranian Red Crescent, with ICRC consignments sufficient for roughly 25,000 people in the initial deliveries. That reporting also noted four Iranian Red Crescent responders had been killed in the war, underscoring the ongoing risk to humanitarian personnel. No new last-24-hour announcement was found indicating a major expansion in aid corridors or funding. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/aid-groups-use-land-routes-to-deliver-humanitarian-relief-to-iran-4612702?utm_source=openai))

The immediate civilian risk today comes less from a newly reported mass-casualty strike than from the possibility of renewed escalation around ports, shipping, and strategic infrastructure. If the ceasefire collapses, displacement and service disruption could rise rapidly again, especially in coastal and logistics-dependent areas. ([icrc.org](https://www.icrc.org/en/news-release/iran-icrc-president-says-return-war-would-be-ruinous-civilians?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The key indicator for May 11 will be whether Iran formally answers the latest US proposal and whether that response includes concrete terms on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Also worth watching are any CENTCOM announcements on escort or interdiction activity, because even a limited maritime clash could quickly reverse the day’s tentative diplomatic stabilization and send oil sharply higher again.

briefingArchive.title: Day 70 Intelligence Briefing — May 9, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development in the past 24 hours is renewed U.S.-Iran maritime combat around the Strait of Hormuz despite the nominal ceasefire framework, with U.S. forces disabling additional Iranian tankers and both sides hardening their public positions. Markets have not repriced to a full-war escalation, but energy, shipping, and diplomatic indicators all suggest the crisis remains one miscalculation away from a broader relapse into sustained hostilities. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/6490db55a65880a61a6233eff7acc68b?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, the conflict picture was dominated by maritime and air action linked to the Hormuz theater rather than a return to the large-scale strategic strike campaign seen earlier in the war. The clearest confirmed event is that U.S. forces disabled two additional Iranian tankers after an overnight exchange of fire with Iranian forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz, according to AP’s reporting on Friday, May 8. AP said the United Arab Emirates also reported another Iranian missile-and-drone attack, indicating the theater is widening beyond ship interdiction into continued pressure on Gulf partners. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/6490db55a65880a61a6233eff7acc68b?utm_source=openai))

CENTCOM’s latest directly accessible official operational detail remains its May 6 announcement that U.S. forces enforced blockade measures against the Iranian-flagged tanker Hasna in the Gulf of Oman. According to CENTCOM, a U.S. Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet launched from USS Abraham Lincoln used its 20mm cannon to disable the ship’s rudder after repeated warnings were ignored. That establishes at least one confirmed weapon system and one operational pattern: air-delivered precision disabling fire against shipping rather than tanker-sinking strikes. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4479004/us-forces-disable-vessel-in-gulf-of-oman-attempting-to-violate-blockade/?utm_source=openai))

Le Monde, summarizing CENTCOM’s more recent account of the May 7-8 violence, reported U.S. “self-defense retaliatory strikes” on Iranian military installations tied to attacks on U.S. forces, including missile and drone launch sites, command-and-control nodes, and ISR infrastructure. However, no authoritative U.S. public damage assessment from the last 24 hours was readily available beyond those target categories. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours were found of fresh deep-penetration U.S. or Israeli strategic strikes on Iranian nuclear infrastructure or major inland air bases. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/05/08/trump-downplays-threat-to-iran-ceasefire-after-exchange-of-attacks_6753250_4.html?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s line remains that Operation Epic Fury as an offensive campaign is effectively over, while current actions are defensive or enforcement-oriented. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on May 5 that Operation Epic Fury “is over” and that a new defensive phase had begun around Strait security, while President Trump and Pentagon officials have argued recent exchanges do not necessarily terminate the ceasefire. That framing allows the U.S. to portray strikes and interdictions as limited enforcement rather than renewed war. ([latimes.com](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-05-05/ceasefire-is-not-over-hegseth-says-as-u-s-acts-to-reopen-strait-of-hormuz?utm_source=openai))

CENTCOM’s public messaging emphasizes professionalism, blockade enforcement, and self-defense. In the Hasna case, it stressed repeated warnings before disabling action. Reporting carried by Le Monde says CENTCOM similarly described the latest retaliatory attacks as directed at launch sites, command nodes, and ISR positions responsible for attacks on U.S. forces. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PRESS-RELEASES/Press-Release-View/Article/4479004/us-forces-disable-vessel-in-gulf-of-oman-attempting-to-violate-blockade/?utm_source=openai))

Iranian state-aligned messaging is almost the mirror image. Press TV has described U.S. actions as “terrorist” or “pirate” violations of the ceasefire, while senior Iranian figures such as parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf argue the United States and its allies have endangered shipping through their blockade and that Tehran still retains substantial escalation capacity. Iranian narratives stress that Iran is enforcing a new maritime order in Hormuz and merely warning or responding to unlawful U.S. encroachment. ([presstv.ir](https://www.presstv.ir/Detail/2026/05/07/768234/iranian-forces-struck-us-vessels-swift-retaliation-tanker-attack-top-command?utm_source=openai))

Israel has kept a lower public profile in the last 24 hours than Washington and Tehran in available reporting, but Israeli reporting and prior U.S. statements still treat Iranian missile, drone, and maritime threats as part of a single regional coercion architecture. The main contradiction is stark: the U.S. says it is protecting navigation and enforcing a blockade; Iran says the blockade itself is the ceasefire violation and that Tehran is defending sovereign and regional security. Both narratives are plainly propagandistic, and neither side has yet offered independently verifiable battle-damage evidence for the newest claims. ([lemonde.fr](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/05/08/trump-downplays-threat-to-iran-ceasefire-after-exchange-of-attacks_6753250_4.html?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

The immediate market response remains one of persistent risk premium rather than panic repricing. Reuters reported on May 7 that U.S. and European stocks slipped while oil swung sharply intraday as investors tried to interpret conflicting signals from peace talks and maritime clashes. Reuters said both crude benchmarks had earlier dropped by as much as $5 a barrel on optimism over a limited arrangement, underscoring how headline-driven pricing remains. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/asian-stocks-hit-record-high-dollar-wobbles-on-peace-deal-hopes-4615955?utm_source=openai))

For exact same-day spot figures on May 9, no reliable direct pricing feed was available through the toolset. The most recent high-quality reporting in the past few days indicates Brent and WTI remain highly volatile and still elevated relative to prewar levels, but below the March-April peak shock phase. Earlier Reuters reporting showed Brent had fallen to $94.79 on April 14 on renewed talk hopes, after trading above $100 during the blockade escalation and above $110 during the war’s most acute supply shock. In other words, the market is still carrying a sizeable geopolitical premium, but not currently pricing a total and prolonged loss of Gulf flows. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-crude-futures-fall-over-1-as-traders-weigh-supply-risks-4611537?utm_source=openai))

Broader macro effects remain centered on inflation risk, transport costs, and energy equities. Reuters has noted that investors are watching oil as the leading signal for how seriously to treat the conflict’s economic drag, while analysts continue warning that any durable supply disruption could flip the 2026 market into deficit. Gold has also been repeatedly identified as a safe-haven beneficiary during escalatory phases, though no confirmed fresh May 9 benchmark price was available in the latest search results. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/persistent-iran-war-energy-price-surge-set-to-loom-over-stocks-4573502?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The shipping picture remains severely disrupted. AP reported on May 6 that hundreds of vessels were still stuck in the Persian Gulf, with operators facing mounting costs and uncertainty over when or whether Hormuz can reopen safely. AP also reported that a CMA CGM container ship was damaged while attempting transit, while major operators continued to judge the strait too dangerous because of Iranian speedboats, drones, and the broader military standoff. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/03af894eaddb8ede53928babc76f80e2?utm_source=openai))

Reuters reporting from earlier this phase said shipping traffic through Hormuz had fallen to a virtual standstill, and Reuters-derived reporting on May 4 said there were still no signs of increased traffic even after U.S. declarations that it would work to free shipping. Additional Reuters-based reporting showed that no LNG cargoes had transited the waterway during key stretches of the crisis and that even loaded Qatari LNG vessels turned back after nearing the strait. That remains strategically important for Asia, where refiners and utilities are more exposed to Gulf crude and LNG disruptions than U.S. consumers are. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/shipping-traffic-remains-at-virtual-standstill-through-hormuz-data-shows-4622861?utm_source=openai))

On consumer behavior, direct past-24-hour confirmation of fresh fuel hoarding in Asia-Pacific was limited. However, Reuters’ timeline material and broader supply reporting indicate that fuel shortages across parts of Asia have already been a recurring effect of the war, and Axios reported this week that gasoline prices are unlikely to return to prewar levels soon even if a deal materializes. The best analytic judgment is that outright panic buying may now be episodic rather than universal, but supply-chain stress, costly rerouting, longer voyage times, and elevated insurance premiums remain very much in place. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours were found of new mass fuel-hoarding waves beyond those established earlier in the crisis. ([reutersconnect.com](https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/timeline-fuel-shortages-across-asia-as-iran-war-drags-on/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX1ZBNTE0NzE4MDMyMDI2UlAx/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX0xWQTAwMzUxNDcxODAzMjAyNlJQMQ?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomatically, the past 24 hours brought movement but no breakthrough. Axios reported late on May 8 that Vice President JD Vance met a Qatari mediator as Washington awaited an Iranian response to its latest peace proposal. Pakistan remains the formal mediator, but Qatar is clearly still active in the background, suggesting a multilayered channel rather than a single-track negotiation. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/08/vance-qatar-mediator-iran-war?utm_source=openai))

At the United Nations, the U.S. and Gulf allies have continued trying to raise pressure on Iran over Hormuz access. AP reported earlier this week that Washington and Gulf partners were pushing a UN proposal threatening sanctions if Iran does not release its chokehold on the strait. That effort follows an earlier, weaker resolution that China and Russia vetoed, an important indication that neither Beijing nor Moscow is prepared to fully align with Washington’s coercive maritime approach. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/fb9532308885dd260bf8f44353d51b0a?utm_source=openai))

UN messaging remains focused on de-escalation, respect for ceasefire obligations, and civilian protection. The UN Office at Geneva said this week that closed-door Security Council talks followed attacks on the UAE and reiterated that resolution 2817 must be respected. António Guterres has consistently pressed for continued talks and an end to ceasefire violations. ([ungeneva.org](https://www.ungeneva.org/en/news-media/news/2026/05/118378/security-council-holds-closed-door-talks-following-attacks-united?utm_source=openai))

The net assessment is that diplomacy is active but brittle. The key question is no longer whether channels exist; they plainly do. The issue is whether Washington and Tehran can reconcile irreconcilable public positions on two core matters: U.S. insistence on navigation freedom and coercive leverage, and Iranian insistence that Hormuz control is now part of the postwar settlement. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/05/08/vance-qatar-mediator-iran-war?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No major new humanitarian data dump covering only the last 24 hours was found, but the humanitarian baseline remains severe and worsening. UN reporting from earlier in the conflict documented extensive civilian harm across at least 20 Iranian provinces, and OCHA’s April 3 update said intense airstrikes had caused high civilian casualties and heavy damage to homes, schools, and health facilities. That same update recorded more than 115,000 civilian units damaged and 23 verified attacks on health care between March 1 and April 2, causing nine deaths. ([iran.un.org](https://iran.un.org/en/313396-islamic-republic-iran-humanitarian-update-no-01-17-march-2026?utm_source=openai))

UNHCR’s latest Middle East emergency material, updated in April and early May, indicates significant population movement connected to the war. Its data platform reported more than 205,000 Iranians arriving in Türkiye and more than 180,000 Iranian nationals returning from Türkiye to Iran between March 3 and May 5, reflecting highly unstable cross-border movement patterns rather than one-directional flight alone. UNHCR has also warned that hostilities and pressure inside Iran could trigger further onward movement of Afghans and Iranians alike. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/emergencies/middle-east-emergency?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC has focused particular attention on medical protection.
